claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy is a non-equilibrium, metastable solid solution with negligible intermetallic content.
Thermal exposure under service-relevant conditions accelerates diffusion-controlled nucleation and growth of intermetallic compounds from the metastable solid solution.
Elevated temperature facilitates diffusion along grain boundaries and defect sites in the metastable matrix.
Enhanced diffusion at grain boundaries and defect sites triggers heterogeneous nucleation of intermetallic phases.
Growing intermetallic phases modify the local chemical and electrochemical environment.
Intermetallics whose chemistry favors a coherent, stable oxide promote formation of a protective passivating scale.
Formation of a protective passivating scale retains or improves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Non-passivating intermetallics can form galvanic couples with the matrix.
Galvanic differences between non-passivating intermetallics and the matrix enhance localized corrosion.
Minor Ti or Mg partitioning may modify the passivating character of emergent intermetallic compounds.
The kinetics of intermetallic formation and evolution of the oxide-film structure dictate the balance between retained oxidation resistance and loss of corrosion protection.
Thermally aged samples should develop intermetallic diffraction peaks that are absent from the initial state.
Under high-temperature oxidative conditions, samples that develop passivating intermetallic phases should form more uniform and adherent oxide scales than the metastable control.
Samples that form passivating intermetallic phases should exhibit improved oxidation resistance relative to the metastable control.
Samples that form non-passivating intermetallics should exhibit increased corrosion rates relative to the metastable control.
A sufficient time-temperature exposure window is required to produce measurable intermetallic nucleation.
